speaker: lancecaughfiel
text: All right. Whenever you're ready. Thank you, Your Honor. May it please the court. My name is Lance Caulfield, and I represent the appellant in this case, Sundara Title. This is a breach of contract case in which the alleged breach of contract was the filing of an interpleader. Now, that interpleader was filed by an escrow agent after the funds that were deposited into the registry of the court became disputed between the purchaser and the buyer in a sales contract. That interpleader cannot be a breach of contract for three reasons. First, because Sundara was not prohibited from interpleading by any contractual provision. Second, because even if there had been a provision that required the withdrawal or return of funds, then interpleader would have fulfilled those contractual terms or it would have resulted in a discharge of liability in regards to any breach of contract. And third, because even if there had been an actual breach of contract, the damages are not supported in this case. And that's, again, for two reasons. First, because the first element of damages was based upon a theory of economic duress and an interpleader cannot be the source of duress as a matter of law. And the second element of damages was attorney's fees, and those failed to withstand the element requirements that are set forth in RORMAS. Now before I address those three primary issues, and there are subsidiary issues in the brief, but those are the three issues that I think are really the most important ones, I'd like to briefly address the amicus, if I could. There was an amicus brief that was filed by the Texas Land Title Association. And the amicus brief points out that escrow agents are in a very unique position when it comes to disputes over funds. In fact, what the amicus brief makes clear is that escrow agents must remain neutral and they cannot explain contractual obligations, much less determine contractual obligations when disputes arise between the parties to which they owe fiduciary duties, equal duties. Now they cite this court to a decision called Bell v. Safeco, a decision from this court, in which this court noted that that neutrality must be maintained to such an extent that it is even inappropriate for an escrow agent to explain the consequences of a contractual provision when they are requested to do so by one of the parties. The amicus also points out that interpleader is essential to the function of escrow agents in Texas because without free recourse to that remedy, there would be additional delay in costs in every closing. Those policy reasons and with the amicus's position in mind, I'll turn to the first issue, if that's appropriate, then there's no questions. And that first issue deals with the breach. In this case, there was no breach because there was no duty to immediately turn over the funds upon demand. Now the amicus, when they cited to Safeco, I looked at cases citing Safeco, I analyzed that decision, and I found a case named Equisource Realty Corporation v. Crown Life Insurance Company that I wish I'd found for my brief. And that decision, which is at 854 SW 2nd 691, a 1993 decision from this court, notes that escrow agents' duties must, quote, be strictly limited to those defined by the escrow agreement. And so we turn first to what were the escrow agents' duties, how were they limited, what were their obligations under the agreements? The first agreement is the purchase agreement. And that contract permitted interpleader. It permitted interpleader of the escrow money. It did not address interpleading the purchase funds because it did not contemplate purchase funds being delivered until closing. Now that purchase agreement is at tab 11, page 20 of our brief. And it was between the buyer and the seller. When Sendera signed it, and that's on page 20 of the purchase agreement, it signed it only to accept the earnest money subject to the terms and provisions of the purchase agreement. And that purchase agreement, under section 16, expressly permitted Sendera to hold the earnest money or interplead it at its discretion in the case of any dispute. As such, there can be no breach of contract for interpleading the funds for the earnest money because it was expressly permitted under the agreement. I'm trying not to speak over it, Justice, and so if I hear a noise, I'm stopping. I apologize. Now the authorities will argue, most likely, that silence as to permission to interplead other funds means you couldn't interplead those funds. I don't see how that's a correct interpretation of the contract under Texas law. Under Texas law, additional provisions should never be engrafted into a written agreement unless they're necessary to the purpose and performance of that agreement. Now here we have a written agreement that expressly permits interpleader, does not mention interpleader for purchase funds. If we're going to engraft a restriction any time interpleader is not specifically permitted in a purchase agreement, then we're really going to throw things for a loop here in Texas because any time anything is deposited with an escrow agent and it's not specifically delineated to have a right to interplead those funds, interpleader will never be appropriate. That's the sort of fear that the amicus is representing in this case. They're afraid of that sort of result. And in fact, that sort of result is contrary to appropriate rules of construction. We cite in our brief the utilitarian rule that says if you have a business contract, then it should be interpreted in a way that makes sense in light of the business that's being conducted. It makes no sense to prohibit escrow agents from ever using Rule 43, a right that they have to use in the form of interpleader, when that function is particularly important to them being able to serve as neutrals. Now, the purchase agreement doesn't prohibit interpleader. And so, athletes have recourse to the escrow instructions.

speaker: lancecaughfiel
text: Anything that is put into the, anything that's entrusted to a third party that doesn't have a claim to it can be interplead under Rule 43. Yes, Your Honor. And when the contract is drafted, it's contracted with acknowledgment of the law, and it expressly permits interpleader under similar circumstances. In fact, Rule 43 only requires that there be conflicting claims. As the Clayton case points out, the other requirements come from the common law. But to get back, if I've answered your question, to get back to the discussion of these escrow instructions, which they claim required return of funds, yes, the escrow instructions define the closing documents that needed to be returned. It did not include the funds in those closing documents that needed to be returned. So claiming that that creates a demand return obligation doesn't comport with the language of the agreements. In fact, the agreements themselves state that the right to withdraw only exists prior to consummation and funding. So the right to withdraw the closing documents is separate from funding. And the inclusion of funds in a definition of purchaser's closing documents in the purchase agreement, and that's in Section 12C, does not contain a return or withdrawal obligation. And so the more specific definition that's found in the escrow letters controls and does not require a return upon demand. Now, Apelli's argument then that there was a breach of contract fails for at least three different reasons. First, because Sindera only agreed to accept the earnest money pursuant to the terms of the agreement. And those terms did not retire the immediate return of any funds. Second, because the more specific supplemental escrow instructions carved funds out of the definition of closing documents that needed to be returned upon demand. And third, because the limitation provisions that we'll probably hear about were between the parties. They were between the purchaser and the seller. And Sidera did not agree to be bound by those provisions. It had no obligation to interpret those provisions. And in fact, doing so would have been contrary to its role. Let's turn then to the second point, which is that even if there had been an obligation to return or pay, then interpleader fulfilled that obligation. Now first, as the PetroSource Partners versus 3B Rattlesnake case discusses, whenever there is a contractual obligation to pay, interpleader fulfills that obligation. And so, whenever you have a functional equivalent of payment in the form of interpleader, like we had here, a contract is not breached. But separate and apart from that, when the only potential liability here is discharged.

And so, Mr. Corey, at trial, asked for an instruction that required that there be a determination of reasonableness. What was given was a requirement that the claims be bona fide. And as our brief discusses, that's not an appropriate requirement under the law. So, that's probably a long-winded answer to your question. But the Rule itself only requires conflicting claims. Texas Supreme Court says they only have to be reasonable. And all questions of reasonableness are determined in favor of the interpleading party.
